newsitem.title: INDIA: India stocks seen quiet, await oil price hike.
newsitem.headline: India stocks seen quiet, await oil price hike.

text.p: Indian shares are seen quiet this week as participants seek clues on market direction amid uncertainity about the timing of a hike in government-set oil prices, analysts and dealers said at the weekend.
But some traders said a technical correction in share prices late last week coupled with renewed fund buying could see the market moving higher.
"There is a lot of pessimism in the market," said Imran Contractor, research head at Shah & Sequeira Investment Advisory Services. "So, any good news could trigger a rally."
Analysts predict a slow reversal of an economic slowdown seen since November 1996 and which has affected performance of a majority of companies.

SocGen Crosby, in its latest South Asia Quarterly economic view, forecast a gradual recovery in the economy in the first half of financial year 1997/98 "based on the recent fall in nominal lending rates and the clearing of credit channels".

Tata Iron & Steel Company (TISCO), Steel Authority of India (SAIL) and Indian Petrochemical Corporation Ltd (IPCL) figured among the latest companies that announced lower profits in the year ending March 31, 1997.
"Our survey with several industries indicate that there has been a distinct pick- up of activity in May, probably indicating an upturn in the economy," Shah & Sequeira said in a report.
"One should pick up blue-chips now," it saidl.
Bombay's benchmark 30-share index rose 48.73 points to 3,755.10 in the week ending Friday, with most of the gains coming in the last few days of the week.
"Basically, we have seen some fair amount of delivery-based buying by foreign funds," said Sandeep Dhingra, equity analyst at SSKI Securities Ltd.
Dhingra said attractive valuations in blue chips might be luring renewed buying by foreign funds.
But, government inaction on a long-awaited decision to increase prices of petroleum products was a market dampener, analysts said.
"We need to see some strong decisions taken by the government," said Kamal Kabra, a member-broker and former president of the Bombay Stock Exchange. "It can't go on like this."
Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral last week said it was inevitable that the government would raise petroleum product prices to tackle a soaring oil pool deficit.
A steering committee of the ruling United Front will meet on June 8 to decide the oil price issue, Gujral said on Saturday.

Analysts said the government must decide soon how to pay money owed to oil companies, which totalled 155 billion rupees ($4.3 billion) at the end of March, for selling subsidised petroleum products well below global prices.
The deficit is expected to rise to 245 billion rupees by March 31, 1998.
"We are an open economy, yet subsidised. This is undermining industrial strength," Kabra said.
